articles.title: AI Policy Lawmakers Exploit Semiconductor Trades Ahead of Stalled Bans
articles.content: LivestreamMenuRep. Josh Gottheimer disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks, including Benchmark Electronics and Applied Materials, as he helps shape Democrats' AI agenda.The New Jersey Democrat's trades came months after Gottheimer voted to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual stocks, a restriction he has supported for years.There's no evidence of wrongdoing, but the investments face fresh scrutiny as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and ramp up oversight of the AI industry.In this article Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat helping write his party's artificial intelligence agenda, has disclosed new purchases of AI-linked stocks — just months after voting to ban lawmakers and their families from buying individual shares. The New Jersey Democrat disclosed an Oct. 12 purchase of between $1,001 and $15,000 of Benchmark Electronics stock, according to a filing released this week. His jointly owned Morgan Stanley account also bought up to $15,000 worth of Applied Materials shares on Oct. 26, following three earlier purchases of leading AI chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices. While there's no evidence of wrongdoing, the trades put Gottheimer's investments in the spotlight as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, gaining new power to regulate and investigate the AI industry. Gottheimer, a former Microsoft executive, sits on the House Financial Services subcommittee overseeing AI in finance, has introduced legislation on AI regulations and co-chairs a commission developing Democrats' broader AI agenda. Gottheimer's spokesman, Haraden Bottomley, said the congressman turned over control of his investments to a third party with "full investment discretion" before taking office in 2017. "Gottheimer is also awaiting approval from Congress of a blind trust. In the meantime, he has taken the extra step of setting up an independent trust," Bottomley said. Democrats are already targeting the AI industry. Reps. Maxine Waters and Greg Casar introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts for AI companies, referred in part to Gottheimer's committee. Casar has also called for AI executives to testify under oath, while other Democrats are pushing to restrict data centers or halt new construction altogether. The purchases also contrast with Gottheimer's longstanding support for restricting congressional stock trading. In July, he was among just 13 Democrats who voted for the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would prohibit lawmakers and their families from purchasing most individual stocks. The bill passed the House but has not become law. Some Democrats opposed it both because it contained a voter-ID provision and because some said it should have gone further in curbing stock purchasing and holding by elected officials. Four years earlier, Gottheimer backed legislation requiring lawmakers to place investments in blind trusts and pledged to establish one himself. The AI purchases are just a small slice of Gottheimer's sprawling investment portfolio. The five trades totaled between $5,005 and $75,000, compared with $15.1 million to $59 million in disclosed household assets, including up to $44.5 million in stocks. His household has reported more than 1,100 securities transactions over three years, according to Follow the Filings. Gottheimer reports household assets jointly with his wife, Marla Tusk, who is general counsel at a political consulting firm. Advanced Micro Devices competes with Nvidia in AI chips, while Applied Materials supplies semiconductor manufacturing equipment. It was also Benchmark's largest disclosed customer in 2025, accounting for 14% of revenue, according to a securities filing. Benchmark, meanwhile, generated 30% of its third-quarter revenue from semiconductor equipment and another 16% from advanced computing and communications, according to its Oct. 28 earnings report. Gottheimer also disclosed an Applied Materials purchase in August and a sale in September. The purchases came shortly before a sharp selloff in AI stocks. The Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.5% Thursday, as Nvidia dropped more than 9% and AMD roughly 17%. The index includes both companies. Benchmark fell nearly 17% over Wednesday and Thursday, closing at $59.34 — roughly 25% below its closing price on Gottheimer's October purchase date — before recovering somewhat Friday.

While co-sponsoring bills to bar lawmakers from trading individual securities, the member accumulated positions directly benefiting from upcoming federal semiconductor subsidies and export controls. The revelation cements public cynicism that technology regulation in Washington is primarily weaponized for personal capital accumulation.

articles.content: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply? by Dylan Furbay - 11/07/26 12:01 PM ET Link copied Link copied NOW PLAYING ( NewsNation ) — A series of cyberattacks on grocery stores out of Europe have raised concerns about cyber threats stateside as the U.S. government warns businesses of potential attacks targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems. Brett Leatherman, head of the FBI Cyber Division, spoke in an advisory warning Thursday , urging organizations to take mitigation steps against potential malicious cyber actors immediately. “These systems protect food and medicine across health care, food and agriculture, and other critical sectors here in the United States as well. Attackers are getting in through controllers that are unpatched, reachable from the internet, or still using the default passwords listed in the manufacturer’s manual,” said Leatherman. In a joint warning from the FBI, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Health and Human Services (HHS) and U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), experts urged organizations to eliminate public internet exposure, isolate operational technology and enforce credential security to mitigate potential attacks. Former FBI Special Agent Nicole Parker spoke with Fox News to warn Americans further, interpreting the cyberattacks as a form of “asymmetrical warfare,” where opponents use unconventional tactics to expose the vulnerabilities of a stronger opponent. “This asymmetrical warfare has a very strong psychological impact, but we’re Americans. We will not falter ever,” she said. Parker also urged citizens to keep food, water, medication and other supplies on hand in case of a wider cyberattack Experts dubbed the most recent month “ Black October ” in reference to the intense wave of software vulnerabilities and high-profile cyber incidents driven by AI. A senior director of product management at Figma wrote in an Oct. 22 X post following a surge in PHP attacks , “In the last 2 days there have been several dozen cyber attacks which, in isolation, would each have been the worst to happen in an entire calendar year.” In late August, at least six American military bases suffered freezer malfunctions, and U.S. cyber investigators partnered with French law enforcement to research the potential hacks. In Europe, over 350 supermarkets and several French blood banks reported temperature rises in cold equipment up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, forcing suppliers to throw out shelves of spoiled food, losses which may cost tens of millions of euros. While the French Blood Establishment said its surveillance systems were triggered and taken offline, no blood products were lost during the attack, with the samples promptly transported to other facilities. The hacks came in two waves, one that hit in the middle of October and another impacting grocery stores just days ago. A top cybersecurity official from Romania characterized the threat as “semi-amateurish,” speaking to the AFP news agency. articles.title: Capitol Hill Lawmakers Mobilize Oversight Against Musk Government Efficiency Ambitions
articles.content: Elon Musk, the Republican megadonor who spent President Donald Trump’s first few months in office clumsily disassembling whatever federal agencies he deemed too woke, poured a lot of money into the 2026 midterms—at least $474 million, according to The New York Times . Voters, however, were less enthusiastic about maintaining the status quo: Democrats are currently projected to win 259 House seats and at least 54 seats in the Senate. As an investor, even if you are capable of comfortably dropping half a billion dollars on an election, this is not the return for which you hope. Among many other things, Tuesday’s results mean that for the first time, Musk could soon face meaningful consequences for some of his actions. And although there are plenty of viable grounds for investigating Musk, there’s no better place for Democrats to start than with the wreckage left behind by the “Department of Government Efficiency,” the Musk-led initiative that slashed hundreds of thousands of federal jobs, wasted billions of dollars in public resources, and by one estimate led to the preventable deaths of half a million children. Musk officially left the administration in May 2025. But for the next two years, Democratic lawmakers must use their newfound power to hold him accountable for the things he did—not just to people, but to the very concept of representative democracy. DOGE took power that the Constitution delegates to the legislature and placed it in the hands of lumbering, semi-employable tech bros who cut off funding for vital programs, gutted administrative agencies that threatened Musk’s bottom line, and demonstrated a startling indifference to security and privacy along the way. This is not just about politics. It is the work of enforcing the law against people who break it. The next time a reactionary billionaire contemplates hijacking the federal government in order to cosplay as a pro-innovation, anti-bureaucracy technocrat, they need to understand that doing so will come with a price. Under the Constitution, Congress has the implied power to conduct “oversight” of the executive branch, which allows it to investigate to ensure that the laws Congress passes are being enforced. Using these oversight powers, lawmakers can do things like hold public hearings, call witnesses, obtain documents, take sworn testimony, and publish findings. The work of conducting these investigations falls to individual House and Senate committees. And if a person does not wish to participate in the process—for a guy like Musk, a pretty good bet—committees can also issue subpoenas in order to compel compliance. To date, Republicans have had little interest in doing any of these things, and instead have used their majorities in both chambers to protect Musk. In June of last year, for example, House Democrats tried to subpoena Musk during a committee hearing in which they happened to outnumber the Republicans in attendance. In response, the presiding Republican, South Carolina’s Nancy Mace, simply suspended the hearing until her colleagues could wrangle enough Republicans to defeat the motion. Already, though, Democrats have made clear their intent to use Congress’s oversight powers when the new Congress convenes in January. “The American people have a right to know the cost, the consequences, and the chaos resulting from DOGE,” said Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, the ranking Democrat on the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, late last month. “There is a web of potential corruption here that needs to be explored.” Sure enough, while votes were still being counted on Tuesday, Oregon Democratic Senator Ron Wyden hinted that subpoenas would be forthcoming in the not-so-distant future. The incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, California Democrat Robert Garcia, framed the stakes in much more practical terms for members of the extended MAGA universe: “LAWYER UP,” he wrote on X, Musk’s own social-media platform. Under federal law , defying a congressional subpoena is a misdemeanor punishable by fines and up to a year in prison. (In 2022, former Trump adviser Steve Bannon was convicted of contempt of Congress after stonewalling the House Select Committee investigating the January 6 riot.) Congress can also enforce a subpoena by seeking a federal court order, which, if granted, subjects a subpoena recipient to the possibility of being held in contempt of court. Finally, if neither criminal nor civil enforcement does the trick, Congress has an “inherent” contempt power that involves deputizing the Sergeant at Arms to literally arrest a recalcitrant party and jail them until they cooperate. As applied to Musk, each of these enforcement mechanisms comes with unfortunate caveats. The task of prosecuting him for criminal contempt would fall not to Congress, but instead to a Trump-appointed U.S. attorney. Given that the Justice Department now functions as a taxpayer-funded law firm that defends the interests of the president and his allies, I don’t expect that a federal prosecutor assigned to this case would take it especially seriously. Trump has also floated the possibility of issuing a preemptive pardon to Musk. This would not affect Congress’s ability to conduct an investigation, but would protect Musk from the specter of federal criminal prosecution based on its findings—and, depending on how broadly Trump phrases such a pardon, from criminal consequences associated with dodging a subpoena, too. Options outside the criminal legal system also have practical drawbacks. Civil litigation takes time, and Musk would have every incentive to drag out the process and hope that Democrats lose interest—or, better yet for him, control of Congress in 2028. Meanwhile, the last time a chamber invoked its inherent contempt power was nearly a century ago, which means that as cool as it would be to watch, Capitol Police officers are unlikely to perp-walk Musk through National Statuary Hall anytime soon. All that said, neither Musk’s cooperation nor his physical presence is strictly necessary for Democrats to have an impact. They can, for example, hold hearings featuring career civil servants whose jobs disappeared overnight because one of the president’s largest donors decided that their agencies should never have existed in the first place. They can take testimony from subject-matter experts who can quantify the real-world harms that DOGE has already inflicted, and will inflict in the years to come. They can elevate the voices of everyday people whose lives were ruined by random twentysomethings who spent months ping-ponging around the federal government, running agency after agency into the ground. Ideally, of course, Democrats end up getting Musk on camera and under oath. But their oversight powers also allow them to try Musk in absentia in the court of public opinion—essentially, to run a Truth and Reconciliation Commission that will make it too costly, both financially and reputationally, to attempt an amoral stunt like this in the future. In the days since the election, Democrats have already started debating what they should do next; given the volume of horrors perpetrated by the Trump administration thus far, there is no shortage of worthy contenders. But in an interview on MS NOW on Wednesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries broadly downplayed the importance of imposing consequences on those responsible. Voters, he asserted , do not want Democrats to “get even,” but instead to “get things done on their behalf.” The premise here—that holding bad actors to account and getting things done are mutually exclusive—is a textbook false choice that, to their credit, other Democrats have been pointedly rejecting . Other than Trump, there might not be a more toxic figure in recent political history than Musk, who over the course of a weekend fed the U.S. Agency for International Development into the woodchipper— his metaphor, not mine —after reading one too many demented conspiracy theories on X. Many of the people who lost their jobs because of DOGE are still looking for work. One study estimated that the cuts to USAID could lead to 14 million additional deaths by the end of the decade. Ensuring that Musk faces consequences for these choices is not “getting even.” It is governing. The voters who rejected Trump and his movement on Tuesday did their jobs. It is time for Democrats to do theirs: to find out exactly what DOGE did, to punish people who broke the law, and to prevent it from happening again. articles.title: Grassroots European Rebellions Block Aggressive Hyperscale Compute Land Grabs
articles.content: Manuel G. Pascual Madrid - 07 nov 2026 - 05:30 CET Compartir en Whatsapp Compartir en Facebook Compartir en Twitter Desplegar Redes Sociales Ir a los comentarios Añadir EL PAÍS en Google Compartir: Whatsapp Facebook Twitter Bluesky Linkedin Copiar enlace Este sábado hay convocadas movilizaciones en 15 países europeos para solicitar una moratoria en la construcción de centros de datos , esas instalaciones repletas de servidores y procesadores sin los que no funcionaría internet y que han florecido en los últimos años de la mano de la irrupción comercial de la inteligencia artificial (IA). España aglutina 22 de las 90 acciones de protesta previstas, que se desarrollarán en ciudades como Barcelona, Madrid, Sevilla y Pamplona. Es la primera iniciativa de este tipo coordinada a escala europea. “Pedimos una moratoria inmediata sobre la construcción de nuevos centros de datos a gran escala a nivel local, nacional y europeo”, resume Aurora Gómez, de 43 años y nacida en Ballesteros de Calatrava, Ciudad Real. Esta psicóloga es la fundadora del colectivo Tu Nube Seca Mi Río y coordinadora de los eventos organizados en España. “Los gobiernos, la UE y las grandes empresas tecnológicas están avanzando a toda velocidad con la construcción de estas instalaciones. Exigimos que se detenga de inmediato este proceso, que se lleve a cabo un análisis exhaustivo de las repercusiones medioambientales, democráticas y sociales, y que se establezcan marcos claros para decidir si deben construirse centros de datos a gran escala y en qué condiciones”, apunta. Países como Irlanda, Países Bajos o Singapur ya han puesto en marcha moratorias de este tipo. En EE UU, que concentra la mitad de los centros de datos del mundo, la carta blanca otorgada a la industria por el presidente Trump ha provocado la reacción de los votantes en las elecciones de medio mandato. Los analistas creen que el deseo de imponer una moratoria y ordenar el crecimiento del sector explica parte del impulso que ha permitido al Partido Demócrata arrollar en los comicios, asegurándose el control del Senado y la Cámara de Representantes, aunque también hay republicanos que comparten esa inquietud . La resistencia ante estas infraestructuras es poliédrica. Sus externalidades negativas son variadas: consumen mucha energía, hasta el punto de subir la factura de la luz en algunas regiones ; generan poco empleo, más allá del necesario para construirlos; necesitan agua , hacen un ruido constante, acaparan y modifican mucho territorio y se sabe también que pueden generar problemas para la salud de los vecinos . Gómez no quiere ver todo eso en España. “En Irlanda, los centros de datos suponen ya más del 30% de la demanda estatal de electricidad, según la operadora Eirgrid. En Latinoamérica han exacerbado sequías. No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie, queremos juntarnos en las plazas públicas y defender nuestra agua, clima y territorios”, sentencia. La vertiente internacional del movimiento es, en su opinión, esencial para su crecimiento. Alemania, Austria, Bélgica, Dinamarca, Finlandia, Francia, Irlanda, Italia, Países Bajos, Polonia y Reino Unido participan también en la movilización. “Llevamos un año pensando en esta campaña, y entendiendo que las movilizaciones de estos días son solo un punto de partida. Cada país tiene unas características diversas, desde el tiempo que llevan implantados los centros de datos hasta la situación política, el estado de sus resistencias o los impactos que más preocupan. Hemos buscado una coordinación plural, donde desde la parte europea se aporten la idea central de moratoria y las comunidades puedan adaptar las demandas específicas y los formatos de acción que mejor encajen”, explica. En España hay convocadas para este sábado 22 movilizaciones de naturaleza muy diversa. “Por ejemplo, habrá manifestaciones más clásicas en Zaragoza, y paseos reivindicativos en Madrid. Pero también bicicletadas alrededor de los centros de datos, medir la distancia del centro de datos a su vivienda, grupos que se juntan a hacer peticiones públicas de transparencia, recitales de poesía o lecturas de fanzines. Cada comunidad elige la manera de protestar que mejor le encaje, que a la vez sirva de punto de encuentro y debate”, señala Gómez. Aunque en países como EE UU el debate en torno a los centros de datos ha entrado de lleno en la conversación pública o incluso en la campaña electoral, en España todavía no estamos en ese momento. Con todo, Gómez detecta un creciente interés en el asunto, acaso alimentado por la animadversión que despiertan los dueños de las grandes tecnológicas. “En los cuatro años que Tu Nube Seca Mi Río lleva como colectivo hemos visto una sensibilidad creciente respecto a los impactos de los centros de datos y una mayor preocupación de los europeos respecto a este tema, como refleja una encuesta que hicimos hace un año”, indica. “La gente en lo rural se está levantando contra los centros de datos, y en las ciudades cada vez están más preocupados por los impactos de la IA. Ambas son dos caras de la misma moneda, y es ese hermanamiento entre las luchas rurales y de ciudad lo que puede dar todo el impulso que necesitamos para parar un problema tan grande”. articles.title: Beijing Expands Transnational Digital Surveillance to Stifle Overseas Dissent
articles.content: Add TT as Preferred Source The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) “overseas police stations” have not been shut down, but are instead expanding in number, with nearly 1,250 formally designated operations in at least 91 countries, human rights organization Safeguard Defenders said in a report released on Friday. The report, titled A Formula for Repression: China’s Global Grid for Community Control, was released at the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China’s (IPAC) annual summit in the Netherlands. The report identified 74 Chinese authorities and CCP bodies operating through 1,247 designated overseas liaison points at the direction of the CCP’s United Front Work Department that are using the offices to monitor Chinese diaspora communities. The number is likely an underrepresentation of actual activity, the report said, adding that Beijing’s claim that its overseas Chinese police stations were closed was false. Safeguard Defenders in 2022 published two reports detailing the activity of more than 100 overseas stations operating in more than 50 countries, prompting many of the countries affected to denounce the illegal operations, with some launching criminal investigations, it said. China later claimed that the stations had been closed, but more than 10 police forces from five Chinese provinces are involved with a global network of CCP operatives, this week’s report said. Since late 2024, five new national policies instructed authorities across China to expand such activities abroad, aiming to export the domestic system of grid management to control Chinese diaspora, it said. The system of mass surveillance, control and suppression is projected through a global grid of “united front”-affiliated organizations or designated offices that provide the infrastructure other Chinese authorities — police, prosecutors, courts, justice bureaus and others — plug into, it said, adding that they are mostly run by the Overseas Chinese Federation. Every liaison office designated and every task carried out by them are breaches of sovereignty, it said, describing them as “transnational repression embodied” and an “active national security threat.” Policymakers should swiftly devise strategies to confront the “superstructure of CCP interference,” the group said. Laura Harth, Safeguard Defenders’ lead on transnational repression and author of the report, said that the operations should no longer be described as police stations, but rather as a “network system.” China’s illegal overseas police stations have not only remained operational, but have continued to expand under the guise of legitimate community services, Harth said. The system threatens the sovereignty of other countries, undermines democratic institutions, and subjects Chinese diaspora communities to widespread surveillance and coercion, creating fear, she said. The CCP’s definition of the Chinese diaspora extends back as far as 10 generations, she said. Anyone of Chinese descent living overseas, including people from Hong Kong and Taiwan, could be regarded by the CCP as an overseas Chinese, making them potential targets of its surveillance network, she said. IPAC warned that the CCP’s overseas interference and transnational repression in democratic countries were growing increasingly widespread, pervasive and harmful. IPAC cofounder and executive director Luke de Pulford said democratic nations should introduce foreign agent registration systems and impose criminal liability for violations. Organizations affiliated with the CCP’s United Front Work Department should be required to register, De Pulford said. Registration and enforcement requirements should follow an organization’s “united front” affiliations, regardless of changes to its public name, he said. Governments should also issue public notices detailing the CCP’s and the United Front Work Department’s activities, strategies, objectives and targets, as well as publish annual national reports on Chinese interference, he said. They should establish channels for affected diaspora communities to report incidents, and engage directly with isolated communities and groups, De Pulford said. Democratic governments and parliaments must resist the CCP’s persecution of specific groups, he said. Government officials should expand formal meetings with Taiwanese elected representatives, pro-democracy dissidents, human rights advocates and vulnerable diaspora communities, he said. They should also publicly confront CCP officials who attempt to suppress these communities, as doing so would be a direct way to defend national sovereignty and improve democratic resilience, he added. articles.title: Berkshire Hoards Record Cash as Institutional Capital Flees AI
articles.content: Investors are seeking shelter from the AI storm in Berkshire Hathaway after shares of the conglomerate had lagged the broader market since Warren Buffett announced his departure as CEO last year. Recommended Video Berkshire’s class B stock is up 13.6% so far this year, beating the S&P 500’s 7.8% gain. The outperformance has come as Wall Street rotates out of once high-flying tech stocks that rode the AI boom. Since Oct. 1 alone, Berkshire stock has soared 14% while the S&P has fallen about 4%. That mirrors other years that saw major market upheaval. Most recently, Berkshire gained 4% in 2022 when the Federal Reserve launched an aggressive rate-hiking campaign that sent the broad market index down 18%. Still, Berkshire’s own closely followed portfolio hasn’t been immune to recent market swings. According to its third-quarter earnings report filed on Saturday, investment gains plunged 46% from a year earlier to $9.4 billion. Berkshire’s top stock holdings remained Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola during the quarter. While a more detailed filing later this month will reveal its precise moves, the quarterly earnings report showed that Berkshire bought $2.4 billion of stocks during the period and sold some $2.8 billion. The company grew its stake in “commercial, industrial, and other” equities by $2.3 billion on a cost basis, and cut its stake in “banks, insurance and finance” by $400 million. Meanwhile, CEO Greg Abel, who took over from Buffett at the start of this year, continued to draw down Berkshire’s massive cash pile and accelerated stock repurchases. It repurchased $9.6 billion of its stock in the third quarter, more than double the pace in the second quarter. And in the first four weeks of the fourth quarter, Berkshire bought back about $2 billion more in stock. With a broad array of firms under the Berkshire umbrella, the conglomerate remains focused on traditional businesses like railroad BNSF, Brooks running shoes, See’s candies, and Forest River RVs. Abel added to that strategy in July, when he agreed to buy home builder Taylor Morrison for $6.8 billion. That broke a long drought without any major acquisitions as Buffett bemoaned the lack of good bargains. Berkshire’s holdings in the traditional economy have paid off. In the third quarter, its railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses delivered strong profits, though insurance underwriting tumbled. That’s as the AI boom has not only supercharged the tech sector but also industries that benefit from the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on data center construction as well as electrical grid upgrades. As a result, U.S. GDP has been running hot, expanding 3.4% in the third quarter, accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter. But the Democratic sweep of gubernatorial races in data center hot spots like Texas, Ohio and Georgia is expected to slow down the AI buildout and the overall economy. articles.title: Google AI Terms Force School Districts Into High-Stakes Compliance Defiance
articles.content: Schools scramble after Google gives AI ultimatum by Lexi Lonas Cochran - 11/07/26 6:00 AM ET Link copied - 11/07/26 6:00 AM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING Schools are scrambling after Google said Tuesday that education leaders need to either accept some AI in classrooms or lose access to its search engine.   School officials trying to push back on an encroaching AI are in a bind. The tech giant dominates search online, and it didn’t give much time for districts to make their decisions. District leaders say a fight would be a big undertaking, but some may be up to the challenge, especially as public outcry after the announcement grows.  Google announced that early next year its Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will automatically be turned off for school districts and administrators will have to choose to opt into the features. However, the company said Search and AI are “deeply integrated”, and it will not be possible to turn on Google Search without accepting AI.   The company is updating its Search feature, so AI Overviews “will offer step-by-step guided learning” instead of instantly giving students the answers, but that does not offer comfort to the public.   “Google is trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools,” New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.”  AI in schools has become a growing issue as parents and school leaders contemplate how to integrate a technology that is increasingly used in the workforce but viewed with extreme skepticism by critics.   New York City is among multiple localities that has banned AI completely for younger students but still makes it available in some capacity for high schoolers.  “It’s a small microcosm of the issue of AI in our world and AI in school districts, and then how school districts operate,” said Clay Lavercombe, freshman principal at Springboro High School in Ohio.  “To change anything in the middle of a school year, big or small, I think is a challenge. I would hope that leaders would consider that, and maybe even Google would consider that — to allow school districts to determine what they want to do, but I’m sure that there’ll be some school districts, big and small, who say, ‘We cannot use Google, and we’ll have to figure something else out,'” he added. But abandoning Google is not as simple as just switching search engines. An estimated 60,000 K-12 schools use Google Workplace, meaning teachers and students have integrated their work in Google emails, sheets and slides, according to Tech & Learning. Around 93 percent of U.S. public schools either use or plan on using Google Chromebooks in classrooms, About Chromebooks reported. “I really think Google risks undermining its own position. They’ve had a tremendous amount of market share, but they’re ultimately forcing these schools and districts to choose between access to the information that they already have and controlling over how students use AI,” said Eric Gibbs, vice president of education at AI detection company Copyleaks, which works with schools around the country on AI usage.   Google did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment. Advocacy groups had been pushing for the company to turn off its AI features on Google Search after discovering the platform would easily complete a homework assignment for students or give them all the answers.  “We were really calling on Google to turn it off, recognizing that was probably the best way to ensure that kids were safe online and that we ensured that AI was not doing homework and schoolwork for kids,” said Yvette Renteria, chief programs officer at Common Sense Media.  “And so, when Google puts out this choice of ‘You can only use Google Search with AI or you don’t use it at all,’ it’s really disturbing because, again, it takes away the opportunity to provide critical thinking skills, which is so important in education,” she added.  A May 2026 Gallup poll said 50 percent of the U.S. workforce uses AI at least a few times a year and 15 percent uses the technology daily. That usage is expected to increase in the future. Schools have tried several times to ban the technology due to cheating concerns, and some teachers have even switched assignments from online to in-person writing to avoid AI.  AI supporters don’t think the fight is worth having. The Google announcement “doesn’t bother me tremendously. I actually think AI is a useful tool. That, but we also have to have to teach our kids how to use AI. It’s a tool that has to be taught, similar to how to use safe internet practices or how to search on YouTube, use YouTube in appropriate ways. But it’s a tool that’s only going to get bigger, and … that genie’s not going back in the bottle,” said Dustin Strickland, an administrator at North Murray High School in Florida.  “AI is here. It’s part of what is going to be part of our students’ lives. So rather than burying our head in the sand, I think we have to learn, have to teach our kids how to use it effectively,” he added.  Add as preferred source on Google Tags AI AI Gemini Gemini Notebook Google Google Google Workplace New York City New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani Ohio Search Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media Inc. articles.content: Insider Your all-access pass to FP By Cameron Abadi , a deputy editor at Foreign Policy , and Adam Tooze , a columnist at Foreign Policy and director of the European Institute at Columbia University. This week’s congressional elections in the United States saw a historic shift toward Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, including wins in traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. But with President Donald Trump still in the White House and Democrats still trying to give shape to their own agenda, the implications for economic policy remain unclear. This week’s congressional elections in the United States saw a historic shift toward Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, including wins in traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. But with President Donald Trump still in the White House and Democrats still trying to give shape to their own agenda, the implications for economic policy remain unclear. Was the election outcome primarily fueled by inflation? What are the implications for the AI industry? And what macroeconomic options do the Democrats now have? Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze . What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter. Cameron Abadi: What is the relationship between a political event of this magnitude and mundane cost-of-living issues, which most Americans seem to have been bothered by? Is this the stuff that political tsunamis are made of? Adam Tooze: The cost-of-living issue, and the continuous shocks of price increases and the felt experience of the exorbitant level of prices, has probably not been as pressing as it is in the current moment in many parts of the U.S. since the 1970s. So at that level, there’s a kind of epochal quality to this. And the other thing surely to say is that nor have we had a government, an administration and a supportive Congress, so blithely refusing to simply take seriously any of those issues in a meaningful way. And it’s that combination, I think, which creates this outcome. It would have been damaging to everyone’s sort of self-understanding as a rational political analyst if something like this outcome had not happened. Because how can you have this level of dissatisfaction over prices and price increases and a government committed to protectionism, to starting a war, to incredibly unequal tax breaks, to promoting a growth model that is so K-shaped, that is so promoting a wealth inequality, and not get a backlash? That would have tested the ongoing debate about whether the ’90s formula, “It’s the economy, stupid”—this would really have put a stake through the heart of that theory with garlic on top if we had not seen this backlash. CA: This kind of epochal shift inevitably sparks debates about new, or renewed, political taxonomies in the United States. The term that is now being used to describe many of the new senators and governors elected by Democrats in unlikely places is “prairie populism.” And I’m curious what that term might mean when it comes to economic policy? AT: Going all the way back to the late 19th century, there has been a brand of radical, challenging, anti-status quo politics, in contrast to socialism, which was populism. Populism came out of the prairie, out of the Midwest of the prairie states of the agricultural constituency, because it was about the way in which the gilded age economy in the United States was rigged in the interests of coastal elites—basically New York and the East coast elite. And that’s the echo that’s being picked up on in this sort of talk. It’s a little exaggerated because there’s a huge difference between present day consumer orientated cost of living type of politics and the sort of radicalism, the deep structural changes that late 19th-century populists were demanding—who were really challenging the fundamental structures of the American political economy of that moment. And I do think that’s one of the fundamental questions for the Democrats right now, is that coming out of the midterms of 2018—which were also a Democratic breakthrough, against the first Trump presidency, though not on the current scale—there was a real sense that the discourse of American politics shifted. You got figures like Jake Sullivan spiraling to the top of the democratic pile on an agenda that was an explicit break in neoliberalism. And I don’t quite know where that goes right now, whether there is a mood on the large part of the Democratic Party to resume that kind of quite more fundamental questioning of the orthodoxies or whether we take all that for granted now and we’re going to just focus on trying to deliver. I think we haven’t quite got the bearings yet of what this victory means. It was predicted, but I haven’t so far seen on the part of the Democrats a kind of coherent, new, comprehensive agenda—even in the sense of defining what its limits would be and how far one wants to go—emerging at this point. CA: Polls suggest that many voters in the United States share skepticism about artificial intelligence and the role it’s playing in the economy, specifically the proliferation of data centers. What is the future of AI potentially with this new Democratic-controlled Congress? AT: It’s been quite something to behold, the anxiety running through Wall Street over the last couple of days and kind of climaxing last night about the potential threat to the data center build out. Because America’s path to the AI future is very compute heavy. It’s all about data center build outs. And if you look at the states where this is happening, apart from Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, I think the central play is Texas. And there was a real lot of big tech money mobilized on this issue of trying to ensure that a group of AI friendly politicians were elected. And on the contrary then, the groundswell of Democratic mobilization was around AI and data centers as kind of a bundling issue, right? It’s about local pollution from the noise and everything else. It’s about local electricity rates and the impact that these huge consumers have on local energy prices. And it’s about AI as AI, its direct role on the labor market. And it’s about AI as the symbol of an irresponsible, unanswerable kind of oligarchy that just stamps itself on the face of American society. And these were a very powerful combination. And I think Wall Street analysts were counting 40 or 41 local referenda, local motions that are being passed. All of which I think went to the anti-AI side. And in Texas, we’re talking about 60 gigawatts of buildouts, so an absolutely gigantic buildout valued at $200 billion, I think. And now the Democrats have a much more powerful hold on Texas politics than any time recently. And as we know, in the regional political economy of the United States, Texas and Florida are two great red state counter-examples to the New York and California visions of America’s future. And so for this break to happen is really very dramatic. And it does form a connection between this electoral result and the market. On the morning after the election, though the S&P 500 as a whole was doing fine, Tesla had sold off, CoreWeave, all of these cloud companies have sold off quite hard. Trump’s media platforms are down, unsurprisingly. So it does look as though there is a selective shakeout happening across stock that are very exposed on the AI issue, very exposed to this blowback and are, in any case, over the last couple of months, looking increasingly fragile from a financial point of view. CA: Democrats are promising to make life for ordinary Americans more affordable, but how they’ll do that is still somewhat of an open question. On a macroeconomic level, could finding a way to lower interest rates be something that Democrats in Congress turn their attention to? AT: I think this is a really interesting question. I mean, there’s a real tension between projects of trying to address the cost of living crisis through concrete interventions on particular prices and market structure and price gouging on drugs and microeconomic policy strategies and the bigger macroeconomic picture. And of course, Congress doesn’t shape that bigger macroeconomic picture. Really except through fiscal policy. It doesn’t have a direct influence on interest rates. If it wants to see interest rates come down, the way to do that, presumably, would be to adopt tough fiscal policy. It doesn’t necessarily mean you slash spending, but you would need to raise taxes and you’d need to actually build a coalition that was willing to do that. And there’s lots of ways of doing that in a progressive way. But that’s not something the Democrats have been keen to do recently, really, is to push redistributional taxes. Or you have to put the Fed in a position where it has no option but to do various very unconventional interventions. Which again is perfectly logical and sensible from a left Keynesian point of view. But it’s a breach of the kind of orthodoxy which the Democrats have embraced all the time outside moments of absolute crisis. So I do think this question of what the agenda of the Democrats is really, macroeconomically, is quite unclear. Because we’re clearly no longer in the Larry Summers Bill Clinton 1990s era. We left that behind in the Biden administration. What the agenda, what the paradigm now is I think is very open-ended. Take the issue of AI. One of the effects of the AI boom is to suck foreign money into the American equity markets. It’s one of the fundamental ways in which the American balance payments now currently balances. If that goes away—and there’s very good reasons for wanting to embrace that as American’s future, slow this down, try and close the two legs of the K-shaped economy—the most likely prediction is that the dollar depreciates, the dollar devalues. And again, you’ll find people saying, Well, that will be great for industrial policy, that’s exactly what we need, American producers are more competitive, who needs tariffs if you have a devaluing dollar? But the dollar is also American purchasing power. And so if the dollar devalues appreciably, seriously, this raises the price of American imports. It raises the cost of buying foreign goods for American consumers. It isn’t a way to increase purchasing power and address the cost-of-living crisis. It does the opposite, right? It restricts imports by way of raising the price of foreign goods. Now, this isn’t one-to-one or simple, but there’s just a series of tensions here that are not squarely addressed at the current moment. There hasn’t been any cause to address them, though I also think there was an agenda around the Biden administration that pretty clearly spelled out some of the trade-offs here. For instance, we would intentionally slow down the renewable energy surge in the U.S. because it involved Chinese solar panels and that wasn’t the top priority, actually. So what are the new priorities? What is the new set? If the cost of living is the absolute priority over everything else, then you would think that a radical free trade agenda would be the way to go. But Congress can’t do that without a compliant White House. And which Democrat is actually going to run on that, given what we know the Biden administration did, which was to maintain Trump’s tariffs from the first administration? And big parts of the Democratic coalition, notably what’s left of the blue collar trade unions, are, shall we say, pro-tariff, broadly speaking. Not Trump’s crazy ones, but they are not interested in ensuring that American consumers can have the cheapest possible affordable family car. That’s not their agenda. So there’s a whole series of really quite complicated trade-offs here that will have to be faced again. This post appeared in FP's The Reading List newsletter. Sign up here . articles.title: Technical Debt in Criterion Platform Exposes Streaming Industry Failure
articles.content: One of the most famous twists in film and television history comes at the end of a Twilight Zone episode titled “Time Enough at Last.” A henpecked nebbish manages to survive the apocalypse in a library, surrounded by all the books he never had the bandwidth to read before—only to immediately shatter his Coke bottle-thick eyeglasses. This cruelly ironic fate captures with cinematic flair the high drama of subscribing to the Criterion Channel— the world’s best streaming library , and one of its worst streaming apps. Just when you think it’s the perfect moment to finally watch The Night of the Hunter for the first time—whoops, the app doesn’t work on your TV . For those who may not be cinemaniacs, the Criterion Collection is a film distribution company that preserves historically relevant films with high-quality restorations, and honors other notable works by inducting them into its rarified canon. Following the 2018 collapse of highbrow subscription streamer FilmStruck , then home to many Criterion offerings, the company launched its own service, the Criterion Channel, the following year. While it doesn’t always have every single Criterion-blessed film on tap, what the Criterion Channel has is a profoundly deep bench of stone-cold classics, deep cuts, world cinema standouts, and offbeat new releases. It’s entirely possible to save untold thousands on film school tuition as a Criterion subscriber just by mainlining the most heralded works in cinema history and listening to director commentary tracks and other supplemental materials that demystify the craft that went into making them. Unfortunately, the Criterion Channel has a tech and product-maintenance problem that stands in stark contrast to the quality of its programming. And as rival streamers focus on churning out original (read: often bad) content rather than amassing the best movies ever made, it may be squandering a golden opportunity. At this moment, a good many subscribers with Samsung TVs have been unable to access the app on their TVs for months. The problem began on September 24, when the Criterion Channel rolled out a major overhaul of its streaming platform, which Samsung smart TV users proved unable to access. The next day, Criterion acknowledged that a replacement Samsung app was under review and promised it would be ready in the coming days; in the meantime, customers could watch through a browser or other streaming devices. The problem dragged on, though. Samsung owners with subscriptions reported that the outage continued through October, with the company vowing to provide an eventual updated app compatible with Samsung TVs. Samsung operates its own smart-TV system called Tizen, so streaming services need to develop compatible apps, test them across TV models, and submit updates for Samsung’s certification. Major streamers like Netflix and Hulu tend to have ongoing engineering and distribution relationships with TV manufacturers to manage that process, and so does Criterion, presumably. In any case, the precise technical cause of the Criterion Channel outage for Samsung users after the recent update remains undisclosed, but it may come down to an issue around compatibility testing or release coordination. Asked about this outage, a spokesperson for the Criterion Channel tells Fast Company , “We’re happy to share that the new version of the Criterion Channel app is now live on the vast majority of Samsung smart TVs.” Remaining supported Samsung models are currently undergoing the company’s app review process and should receive the update soon. The spokesperson attributes the delay to Samsung’s review and publishing procedures, which are outside Criterion’s control and have taken longer than anticipated. This isn’t the first time, however, that Criterion Channel subscribers have had technical issues. It’s not even the first time for Samsung owners, specifically. (Samsung did not immediately respond to Fast Company ’s request for comment.) In January 2025, an update reportedly caused the app to crash on Samsung smart TVs whenever users tried to play a film. Some subscribers could still watch Criterion 24/7 —a continuous livestream of curated films the Criterion Channel offers—but choosing any individual movie caused the app to quit. While the compatibility issue was largely resolved by March 2025 , some users reported the bug continued long afterward. for like six months the criterion channel app just wouldn’t work on my samsung tv. I would open it and try to play something and it would just return an error code. anyway it’s back to working now and I still think that was $60 well spent this service rules lol — Bobby Wagner (@bwags) August 25, 2025 Unfortunately, the streamer has been plagued with similar issues practically from the start. In April 2019, not long after the service launched, a Gizmodo writer spent a week with the Criterion Channel , concluding that its fantastic film library was hampered by subpar tech. Chronicling some of the service’s glitches, the author wrote: “ Tokyo Drifter cut off five minutes early for no real reason, Stalker and Paths of Glory both obstructed their final minutes with an error code overlay. (The films played unabated in the background, albeit with a huge ‘COULD NOT PLAY VIDEO’ window over the center of the frame.) At work, it spat back the message ‘Sorry, this video cannot be played while your device is connected to this external monitor.’” Any new streaming service might encounter early issues while stumbling out of the gate, but some of the problems have proven persistent for the Criterion Channel, which as a matter of principle declines to share revenue figures or employee count. (Online data aggregators estimate the company has around 100 employees, and the market intelligence firm Kona Equity estimates annual revenues in the low seven figures.) The user interface remains awkward, for instance, with film descriptions truncated, requiring an additional click on an encircled “i” for “information” in order to read them. The video player has been known to sometimes get stuck buffering and freezing. Users have complained about the difficulty of logging in on Roku devices or the Apple TV app , and some subscribers have been subjected to frequent forced logins . When I mentioned to a movie podcaster friend that I was writing about the Criterion Channel’s tech issues, he complained that the app doesn’t work with his LG OLED TV, and that he has to use his phone app to play movies on it. A quick search online revealed other people had similar issues with their LG TVs . Why do these issues keep coming up? It probably has something to do with the fact that the Criterion Channel is a relatively small, boutique streaming service, and it’s competing with platforms backed by tech giants like Apple and Amazon, not to mention Netflix, which has the resources to ensure a seamless browsing and viewing experience. With presumably much less money and staff to devote to testing and maintenance, it becomes much harder to maintain reliable usage across Samsung, Roku, Apple TV, and all the web browsers. It’s understandable that the Criterion Channel has not grown enough in just seven years for its tech to stand shoulder to shoulder with industry leaders. It’s also a shame—especially right now. If ever there was a moment for the Criterion Channel to explode in growth and become a major player in the streaming wars, it’s this one. Netflix is bleeding relevance , with viewers seemingly unengaged by disposable small-screen blockbusters starring Chris Evans . Streaming’s undisputed titan spends the majority of its content budget on original films, rather than fortifying its library with, say, widely acclaimed arthouse fare and more works from cinematic masters. There is definitely an open lane right now for a scrappy alternative dedicated to arty movies from master directors. Which streamer is better suited to the task than the Criterion Channel? It’s certainly got the goods. Whichever entries from the massive Criterion Collection are absent on the streaming service any given month might rotate back in the following month, in one of its impeccably curated, themed collections. (Recent examples include “ Rock Biopics That Don’t Suck ,” “ Starring Harry Dean Stanton ,” and “ Yearning ,” the last of which you’d better believe includes a pristine print of Wong Kar-Wai’s In the Mood for Love .) Meanwhile, the Criterion brand has never been hotter . The company has recently been riding a late-digital-era appreciation of physical media to high sales , its merch has become a marker of good taste, and celebrities like Charli XCX and Bowen Yang are lining up to get inside the ever-viral “Criterion Closet.” As more and more Criterion fans get funneled into the brand’s streaming service, the Criterion Channel has an opportunity to distinguish itself as the must-have app for serious movie-lovers and those who aspire to be one. But it would help if those fans consistently enjoyed their experience once they got there. The early-rate deadline for the World Changing Ideas Awards is Friday, November 13, at 11:59 p.m. PT. articles.content: The case for managed inference, or automatically routing queries to the right model for the right job Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published sat 7 Nov 2026 // 15:00 UTC Make us preferred on Google Darkbloom, which allowed Mac users to rent out their GPUs for AI inference, warns of low payouts 8 days ago Apple defies memory shortage with new Mac minis August 25, 2026 Conjure cash with old Macs by linking them to AI inference Borg August 24, 2026 Intel bit off more than it could chew with 18A process node June 3, 2026 Argonne flexes spare supercompute to build private AI inference service May 27, 2026 Fireworks AI is fine with helping companies run AI models in their own datacenters, though VP Rob Ferguson argues against doing so. Ferguson told The Register in an interview that while Fireworks AI, a managed inference provider, supports on-prem AI, "we're trying to push people more and more away from it because frankly, it's just the economics." The GPU hardware is just so expensive that if you can't keep it fully utilized, it's a waste of money, he contends. Ten thousand GPUs, he said, represent a billion dollars of capital. "You don't want those things to be sitting idle," he said. For companies with particularly sensitive workloads, Ferguson said, Fireworks is happy to work something out – it offers a service called Sovereign for just that purpose and it has partners like Microsoft that can help. But most inference work probably doesn't need that level of protection, he said. "The state of the art for everyone is to have a portfolio of models," he explained. "In fact, I think most people don't know that the best model in the world's not Astra. The best model in the world's not Fable. The best model is literally a portfolio and we can prove it. You are always better routing between a few models than to do one singular model." That's what Fireworks does through Nexus and its API, alongside competitors like Together AI, Baseten, and DeepInfra. As a managed inference platform, Fireworks AI routes inference tasks to whichever model, frontier model subscription, or API is best suited to handle them. But the company is not just doing naive routing like an AI gateway. It's evaluating tasks as they come in and directing them to the optimal model. "We build custom routers," Ferguson explained. "Our auto model is continuously updating so that we actually go through and we grade the difficulty of the task and we see if there're affinities that the models have, like Kimi is slightly better at JavaScript than Python, things like this." The company's competitive edge, he contends, is its crack engineering team, which follows from its founders' work on PyTorch, a widely used open source machine learning library. "We're performance experts both on the training and inference side," he explained. "People I think don't understand how important, for example, numerics is. So when you use a model, it's always called a mixture of experts – an expert is a different machine. "And so you have all these different machines. It actually matters when you're training that you go back to precisely the right machine, because if you don't, the other machine will still answer the question, but it'll answer in a slightly different way. So we have to know how to build the topology to write back the data to the right space. We have to understand floating point precision [to handle very small values]. We have to be able to do all this where we're routing through a complex fabric through potentially more than one provider depending on what everything is. And so we're really systems experts." Hyperscalers, he argues, will give you a GPU but then it's your responsibility to put it to use. Fireworks' advantage involves being able to maximize utilization at scale while maintaining model precision and speed. Ferguson said AI keeps coming back to economics. "People are just trying to figure out more and more things to use AI for and [to answer questions like] just how much more can I send to cached models, how much more can I send to open models, when do I need this specialization?" he said. "So we're constantly working with customers to help them come up with their own evaluation criteria." One reason for this, Ferguson explained, is that frontier model companies are not transparent about their caching rates. He said Fireworks was working with a data science company and was caching about 90 percent of the tasks. "We looked at [Anthropic's] Opus and it was caching 30 percent of the time," he said. "It was doing AI rework constantly. And with AI, rework is by far your biggest cost. If it's not hitting a cache, then your costs are absolutely insane. And so the token cost is not the real cost. It's the cost per task. And they're hiding that from you. And so we always tell our customers to be tracking cost per task, because that's the real number." Another factor that companies should consider in their cost calculations, Ferguson suggested, is the value of their data and whether they're giving that data away for training. "I think people grossly underestimate the value of their data," he said. Fireworks AI has a zero data-retention policy, "but a lot of times," Ferguson said, "these other companies [do] not, and you should be getting paid for your data. Nobody really knew at the beginning of this current era that these models are memorizers. But now there's plenty of evidence that these models are. So if they're going to be using your data, then you should be getting value for it." But it's not just about cost. Speed, said Ferguson, is underappreciated. "Speed is the thing that people often don't know they can ask for," he said. "It's such a game changer for me and how I work with AI is so different when the responses come back as fast as I ask them." What's the advantage of model ensembling, as the company refers to its model routing activities? A bill that's at least 50 percent smaller, Ferguson claims. "So we say six to eight times cheaper," he said. "The reality is that because a lot of folks have a preference in their tooling, we kinda guarantee that in the case where you're still using a combo of closed and open models, we can always guarantee that your bill will drop by half right away. Like we're sure about that. And then the question is can we just get you to use more stuff?" ® ai and ml ai inference cloud ai Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Meta Strategy Chief Flees Hyperscaler Bureaucracy for Fireworks AI
articles.content: LivestreamMenuMeta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner is leaving the company to become CFO of Fireworks.Fireworks is an AI inference and model-training platform that helps companies customize and run open models.Fireworks was valued at $17.5 billion in a July Series D and is in early talks to raise again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation, Business Insider reported.In this article Dave Wehner, Meta's chief strategy officer, is leaving the company for four-year-old AI startup Fireworks. At Fireworks — an AI inference and model-training platform focused on open models that was valued at $17.5 billion during a Series D fundraising round in July — Wehner will assume the CFO role, he announced on X on Friday. Wehner will be tasked with scaling the company's finances and operations, Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao said in a statement to CNBC. "Fireworks has the right mission for the moment," Wehner wrote on X, adding: "I've become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There's a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need." The AI startup, founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, is a platform that lets developers customize and run open models for their businesses. Its latest investment round was led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV, but Fireworks is also backed by Nvidia and Sequoia Capital. Business Insider reported that it is in early talks to raise funds again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation. Wehner joined Meta, then called Facebook, in 2012 and was the company's chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022. "Dave helped guide Meta through tremendous growth and complexity over 14 years, and brought disciplined thinking to some of our hardest company-level decisions," Meta COO Javier Olivan said in a statement to CNBC. Fireworks is notably smaller than Meta — the tech giant has about a $1.56 trillion market capitalization as of Friday's close — and its competitors, which include OpenAI and Anthropic. "Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again," Fireworks' Lin wrote in a LinkedIn post on Friday. "He sees AI as the defining technology shift of his lifetime and wants to help shape what comes next." The company's size has not made it immune to the risks and complications often associated with AI technology. In October, the company found "a security incident involving unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials," in which "an unauthorized third party accessed environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts," it said in a press release. "Based on our investigation at this time, we have not detected evidence of unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, training data, personal information, or inference traffic within the Fireworks security perimeter or control," the release said.

articles.content: 본문 미국·중남미 트럼프, 격투기 UFC 회장에 백악관 대변인 제안…“좌파 막아야” 김원철 기자 수정 2026-11-08 07:53 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 전·현직 UFC 챔피언 6명을 보좌진으로 데려올 것을 요청 법무부에는 ‘탄핵 위협’ 민주당 상원 의원 등 즉각 수사 지시 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령이 지난 8월 5일 미국 네바다주 라스베이거스의 레드록 카지노 리조트 앤드 스파에서 열린 행사에서 데이나 화이트 유에프시(UFC) 회장 겸 최고경영자(CEO)와 대화하고 있다. 라스베이거스/AP 연합뉴스 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령이 7일(현지시각) 종합격투기 단체 유에프시(UFC)의 데이나 화이트 최고경영자(CEO)에게 백악관 대변인직을 제안했다고 밝혔다. 중간선거 참패 직후 강경파인 스티븐 밀러를 새 비서실장으로 발탁한 데 이어 격투기 단체 수장까지 대변인 후보로 거론하면서, 야당인 민주당과의 대결에서 물러서지 않겠다는 메시지로 해석된다. 트럼프 대통령은 이날 소셜미디어 트루스소셜에 “난폭한 파이터이자 전사인 위대한 데이나 화이트에게 미국 대변인직을 제안했다는 사실을 기쁘게 발표한다”고 적었다. 그는 화이트에게 이슬람 마카체프, 하비프 누르마고메도프, 저스틴 게이치, 대니얼 코미어, 아만다 누네스, 케일라 해리슨 등 전·현직 유에프시 챔피언 6명을 보좌진으로 데려올 것을 요청했다고 밝혔다. 이들 중 일부는 미국 출신이 아니라고 언급한 트럼프 대통령은 “광기 어린 좌파로부터 우리를 지켜줄 이 사람들이 필요하다”며 “데이나는 누구와도 비교할 수 없는 대변인이 될 것이다. 데이나, 제발 이 자리를 맡아달라”고 덧붙였다. 화이트는 트럼프 대통령의 게시글을 자신의 인스타그램에 공유하면서 백악관 브리핑룸 연단에 선 자신의 인공지능(AI) 생성·편집 이미지와 함께 “다음 장으로”(On to the next chapter)라는 글을 올렸다. 그러나 시엔엔(CNN)은 사정을 아는 소식통을 인용해 화이트가 이 제안을 거절했다고 보도했다. 한 백악관 참모는 시엔엔에 트럼프 대통령이 농담한 것이라고 말했다. 반면 연예전문매체 티엠지(T​​MZ)는 화이트가 9일 트럼프 대통령과 백악관 집무실에서 만나 제안을 논의할 예정이라고 전했다. 화이트는 트럼프 대통령과 25년 가까이 친분을 이어온 오랜 측근이다. 트럼프 대통령의 격투기 사랑도 유명하다. 올해 6월14일에는 미국 독립 250주년과 자신의 80번째 생일을 기념해 백악관 남쪽 잔디광장에서 유에프시 경기를 개최했으며, 화이트도 행사 준비에 참여했다. 화이트는 2016년, 2020년, 2024년 공화당 전당대회에서 트럼프 대통령을 지지하는 연설을 하기도 했다. 이번 발언은 트럼프 대통령이 공화당의 중간선거 참패 이후 백악관 핵심 참모진을 교체하고 있는 가운데 나왔다. 트럼프 대통령은 전날 수지 와일스 백악관 비서실장의 후임으로 대규모 이민자 추방 등 강경 정책을 주도해온 스티븐 밀러 백악관 부비서실장을 발탁했다. 트럼프 대통령은 이날 별도의 트루스소셜 게시글에서 민주당이 행정부 인사들에게 탄핵을, 공화당 후원자들에게 투옥을 위협하고 있다고 주장하며 이를 “범죄적 갈취”라고 비난했다. 그는 엘리사 슬롯킨 민주당 상원의원 등을 직접 겨냥하며 법무부에 민주당의 위협 행위를 즉각 수사하라고 지시했다. 트럼프 대통령이 중간선거 패배 직후 강경파를 백악관 비서실장으로 발탁하고 격투기 단체 수장을 대변인 후보로 공개 거론한 데 이어 민주당에 대한 수사까지 지시한 것은 향후 민주당이 장악한 의회와의 대결에서 강경한 대응 기조를 유지하겠다는 신호로 풀이된다. 트럼프 대통령은 7일(현지시간) 트루스소셜에서 데이나 화이트 UFC 회장에게 백악관 대변인직을 제안했다고 밝히면서 격투기 선수들을 보좌진으로 데려올 것을 요청했다고 말했다. 사진은 트럼프 대통령의 게시글에 함께 올라온 화이트 회장(위쪽)과 격투기 선수들의 모습. 트루스소셜 갈무리 워싱턴/김원철 특파원 wonchul@hani.co.kr

articles.title: Tokyo Overhauls Anti-Stalking Legislation to Ban Digital Location Abuse
articles.content: Advertisement Japan This Week in Asia Health & Environment Japan rethinks its stalking laws after Pokemon store murder 4 -MIN READ 4 -MIN Listen Julian Ryall in Tokyo Published: 9:00am, 8 Nov 2026 Long before Moe Harukawa was killed, she lived in fear. The 21-year-old shop assistant had reported her ex-boyfriend to police and a court had ordered him to stay away from her. Yet weeks later, Taiki Hirokawa, 26, walked into Harukawa’s workplace – a packed Pokemon store in Tokyo’s Ikebukuro district – and stabbed her repeatedly in the neck and torso before turning the knife he was carrying on himself. Both later died in hospital. Harukawa’s gruesome murder in March at the hands of a man who had already been arrested and charged with stalking her has stirred debate in Japan on how to stop such fixation-driven attacks.
articles.summary: Japan's government is overhauling its anti-stalking legal framework following a fatal attack outside a Pokemon store facilitated by unauthorized digital surveillance.
